newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Metals trade eyes Chile mine strike, but unruffled.
newsitem.headline: Metals trade eyes Chile mine strike, but unruffled.

text.p: Asian base metal dealers said on Tuesday the strike at the world's biggest copper mine in northern Chile has had no impact on business in the region, but they were keeping a wary eye on the simmering dispute.

"I don't see any panic buying coming in," a senior dealer for a metal trading company told Reuters. "But this sort of situation gives some concern to physical metal availability. People are more cautious about their futures positions."
The general manager for a Japanese metal trading firm said any impact from the strike by 350 of the 2,000 workers at Chile's Escondida copper mine may be felt in the United States.
"It's not having an impact in Asia so far," he said.

Metal brokers Brandeis said in its daily review that the strike in Escondida "served to underpin prices" in the London Metal Exchange (LME), with three-month copper ending on Monday at US$2,290/93 a tonne.
The red metal was seen by regional dealers a touch easier at 0320 GMT at $2,288/93 a tonne.
"I think copper prices on the LME are still weak. I think it will stay in a range of $20 up or $30 down," one dealer said.

Mine officials at Escondida said on Monday the strike has slowed down operations slightly but that output of both cathodes and concentrates remained normal. The workers went on strike last Friday to press for progress in wage negotiations.
The mine is owned by Australia's Broken Hill Proprietary and RTZ Corp Plc of Britain.
Lead prices are also seen dipping further after touching $624 a tonne on Monday, the lowest level since October 1995.
"There is a perception that $600 is the bottom of the range. But there is very good consumer buying around for lead," a dealer said.
"The market found support around $620/$625 but if this comes under fresh attack, we could see prices test the $600 level," Brandeis said.
But another trader said lead is "due for a technical bounce this afternoon. Some people think it's due to go up."
The base metal trade around the region remained quiet, except for what dealers called routine business.
"Most people seem pretty well covered for now," one said.
Dealers predicted a further steady decline in LME stocks with copper tipped to fall by about 2,000 tonnes and aluminium by between 1,000-2,000 tonnes.
"We don't pay too much attention to it now, but the trend is still down," a dealer said.
Most of the dealers pegged premiums for Grade A copper cathodes at around $20-$30 a tonne although one dealer said he heard a range of $30-$50.
"I doubt if anybody would buy at that level," a trader said.
